items.content:
What's left for humans in a world where machine intelligence has so many advantages?

I recently got a Tesla, and using full self-driving has been a wake up call to just how many advantages AI has over humans. The few times I disengaged it because I thought it was going into the wrong lane, it turned out that the car was right and I was wrong. I realized that there is no hope of me driving better than a neural net that knows every road, sees in every direction at once, and never gets tired or distracted.

Given that AI has certain inherent advantages over human intelligence, what kind of moats will remain for us as humans? It's a big question.

One short-term answer is that the world we live in was created for humans, and in some domains, AI has not closed the gap yet. For instance, AI still struggles to use internet user interfaces. While any computer-literate human can navigate a web page with ease, AI is still not great at making accurate clicks and drags because image embeddings are not optimized for such precision. If the internet were designed to be fed into language models instead of rendered as visual interfaces for humans, AI would obviously far exceed humans. But for now, language models still need to be retrofitted to our legacy infrastructure.

Robotics is another area where we humans have a home-field advantage. Most tasks in the physical world are designed around fingers and opposable thumbs, which have been pretty hard to build into robots so far. While it is clear that machines can outperform humans in environments optimized for automation, like large-scale manufacturing lines, for now, most of the world is still built for humans.

However, these capability gaps are only temporary. There will surely be a day when machines click faster than us and have superhuman general dexterity. What are the real moats that humans will have?

Anything involving private knowledge that language models do not have access to feels like a solid moat to me. Romantic matchmaking and high-end real estate are two examples where inventory is often not advertised publicly and matches are made through being in the right circles. Venture capital is another example—although some research and decision making can be automated with AI, much of success hinges on understanding trends ahead of time and connecting the right people, both of which require private knowledge. While machines can and probably will have increasing access to some types of private knowledge, I think there will still be some types of private knowledge that only humans know. I do not see a path for AI to win when critical knowledge is closely guarded in human circles.

A second area where humans seem to have a real moat is in entertainment and the arts, which are inherently valued for their human aspects regardless of how well machines can do them. Watching Usain Bolt sprint one-hundred meters is beautiful as an expression of the peak of human ability, even though cars can drive much faster. Watching chess at the amateur or intermediate level is more relatable and satisfying than watching two superhuman AIs play each other. The value of art comes from the creation process, which is why replicas are not as valuable as originals. These types of work feel like they will continue to have markets even as we advance towards superintelligence.

More broadly, human presence is a feature that will be, by definition, challenging for AI to automate. For example, a teacher remembering your name or a parent supporting you is valuable even though AI can easily remember your name and probably give better life advice. Someone spending part of a finite life on you counts because their time runs out. As a personal anecdote, I remember the first time I worked with someone who I considered an amazing AI researcher. His advice was solid but what was more important was that I believed I could do great work with him as a collaborator and I raised my own standards. Over the past decades, the development of technology has divided us in some ways, but hopefully AI brings us closer to a world where human presence is reemphasized.

Intelligence has been the defining feature of humans and it will be a big change for AI to automate that over the coming decades. In the near term, certain types of intelligence will become very cheap and automate away old jobs, but the moats I described above will not be the only places where humans can hold value. In the same way that computers took away the jobs of secretaries and manual accountants but created far more jobs via the IT industry, I believe there will be much more demand for services created by productive AI-augmented humans, perhaps for services we cannot yet imagine in today’s society. Just seeing how this story plays out will be an adventure in its own right.

items.content:
A few years ago, when I started my AI textbook, I would've guessed AI models would've maybe made it irrelevant at the time of publishing (now in 2026) due to them getting way better at a fairly simple task. I was surprised to be wrong.

Today, models haven't gotten much better at non-fiction/technical writing in long-form. This has me worried for AI models' abilities to do genuine open-ended science, one of the core posited benefits of models. Yes, the models can solve known math problems etc. and make awesome connections across fields, but how are they going to build a literature themselves without massively increasing entropy? Being able to write and organize thoughts is crucial to advancing collective knowledge.

I’m sharing how I came to be worried about this in my latest piece on AI & writing.

items.content:
We wrote a 36-page ArXiv whitepaper on ExtractBench 🧑‍🔬 , our effort to create the most comprehensive, schema-guided, real-world document extraction benchmark.

It’s extremely detailed and covers everything from comparisons with related work on document extraction, to the dataset construction / how ground-truth is generated, to our experiments over 14+ extraction systems.

Here are some of the most salient points from the paper:
✅ The benchmark scores schema-guided extraction on real enterprise documents. Given input doc + schema and predicted output from an extractor, the benchmark measures value accuracy, grounding, tags for each “challenge”, and cost.
✅ Compared to other benchmarks, we have more schemas, more evaluation dimensions, and more data domain diversity
✅ The ground-truth is constructed according to 3 doc subtypes: real-docs use a model ensemble + human review, synthetic long lists have ground-truth by construction, and scanned forms also have human review incl. boxes
✅ Our three modes (LlamaParse cost-effective, agentic, and agentic plus) are at the Pareto frontier of accuracy and cost.

The full ArXiv paper is here: https://t.co/s5azzQV8zr

Our site: https://t.co/VapjcfKCc3

Why do so many AI-powered phone agents sound smart until you interrupt them?

Even when these agents...
items.content:
Why do so many AI-powered phone agents sound smart until you interrupt them?

Even when these agents give you reasonable answers, you still leave these calls feeling like you spoke with a machine that was reading one sentence at a time.

We still haven't built voice agents that feel real.

The problem is that traditional text-to-speech treats every line the agent generates as a separate job.

TTS models don't retain the tone, pacing, or context of the sentence that came before.

That's why voice AI is still so awkward.

Deepgram just released Flux TTS to solve this problem:

Flux TTS is a streaming, conversation-native voice model with a single goal: To retain context across agent turns, so your conversation can stay responsive, consistent, and feel natural.

From what I can gather, there are 3 highlights:

1. Flux TTS remembers the conversation and carries tone, pacing, and context across different turns.

2. It streams in real time with latency as low as 80ms.

3. It handles interruptions and can resume naturally after you cut in.

If you are building a voice agent, check out Flux TTS to help your agent maintain context and respond more naturally throughout a conversation:

https://t.co/ysTbsUerP3

Thanks to the @DeepgramAI team for partnering with me on this post.

items.content:
18 two-word AI prompts I'm kind of obsessed with:

1) now what - great for when you've wrapped up a project or big push and you still have energy and want AI to give you more

2) plz fix - usually accompanied with a screenshot flagging an issue or error or a DM with a bug report

3) do this - usually accompanied with a photo or a screenshot, if I see a great tweet that I want to implement, i'll just screenshot it and toss it to codex/claude

4) interview me - I'm a context hunter, and I want AI to keep pulling more context out of me that I didn't think to first give it, very helpful for tailoring responses or solutions

5) keep going! - I don't know, guys. I just find myself motivating my AI agents a lot more these days. Other versions of this include 'have fun' and 'I trust you'

6) elii elie - this is my shorthand for "explain it to me like I'm an intern" and "explain it to me like I'm an executive" and it's really helpful to get quick reframes if I'm stuck 

7) first principles? - sometimes I read an answer and think 'hmmm that's factually right, but it lacks heart and no one will care' and it's usually because the problem-solving wasn't upstream enough, this prompt helps reset that and reset assumptions

8) simulate it - love when AI runs scenarios, plans for edge cases, and visualizes it all into a dynamic interface for me, this is one of my favorites

9) challenge me - or 'challenge this', used when I desperately need a sparring partner and not a sycophantic kiss-ass :) helps to get a new perspective

10) da fuq? - Fable 5 took a different English class than I did because sometimes that model gives me five paragraphs of hyperdense phd-level info and I'm more lost than when we started

11) find leverage - show me the small moves that create disproportionate outcomes because I don’t always have time to optimize the 37 tiny things

12) hey simon - he's my AI chief of staff, and when I talk directly to him, he can route to and coordinate with the other 33 agents, this is the ultimate 'summoner'

13) spawn agents - any time I'm dealing with massive quantity (like tons of tasks or a lengthy spreadsheet or something), I aim for parallelization. dynamic workflows in claude is another great option 

14) automate this - many times, after a long conversation with AI, I realize that I will need to do that task a whole lot more. So I type something like 'automate this' or 'codify this' or 'schedule this' so it can become a repeatable pattern

15) remember this - any time I flag a mistake or critical context, I'm forcing the AI to log it into memory. It often does it automatically, but not always!

16) forecast impact - asks AI to play out the downstream consequences (including legal, PR, economic, political, team) of whatever I'm asking 

17) show receipts - I want to see solid sources, evidence, reasoning, so I can quickly call out issues (bad sources is a 'fail', and great sources are not an immediate 'pass')

18) girl bye - when AI loses its mind, and I need to get the heck out of there and start a new thread

items.content:
Despite its complex name, a decision coherence system has a simple goal: helping different teams make choices from the same business context.

AI brings shared information and visible trade-offs into the conversation before decisions are made.

Microblog @antgrasso #EnterpriseAI

Consider a common situation.

Sales wants to promise faster delivery, while operations is already working close to capacity.

Both teams may be making reasonable choices, but they are looking at different parts of the business.

A decision coherence system can surface that dependency before the promise reaches the customer.

It shows where assumptions differ and which constraints need attention.

Outcomes from previous decisions can also guide what the organization does next.

People still make the final choice.

AI provides a common view, so local priorities do not create problems elsewhere.

For this to work, organizations need consistent data definitions and clear responsibility for the information feeding the system. Otherwise, they may coordinate decisions more quickly without making them more coherent.

Decision coherence does not require everyone to agree.

It requires everyone to begin from the same business reality.

sometimes you'd rather not see someone's content, or have them see yours.
now you can make that happen in two taps on the https://t.co/UCt2gUhpUs app and web.

📝what blocking does:
block someone and their Characters, Posts, Voices, and Scenes won’t be shown to you, either on search results, the home page, or their profile.

it works both ways, so your content is hidden from them too. they won't be notified.

👉how to do it:
1. go to their profile
2. tap the ... menu
3. tap Block

changed your mind? unblock from their profile, or find the gear icon on your own profile and navigate to Settings > Blocked, where you can manage everyone you've blocked in one place.
blocking and unblocking work instantly, any time. 

now live for everyone.

Good luck to Islam Makhachev, Khabib & team this weekend at UFC 330!

items.content:
Skyr is minimally processed

I recommend using the NOVA scale, it's a great way to figure out if your food is clean or not, and essentially if you should be eating or not

Just take a pic and ask AI what NOVA scale your food is

I generally flat out avoid eating from groups 3 and 4 nowadays (except cheat days once in a while ;))

What's interesting is that a lot of the food that used to be NOVA 1 (unprocessed) a few decades ago has now become NOVA 4 (ultra processed) due to inflation

The reason is that unprocessed food is cheap and boring and hard to market, so you can't make much profit on it. A steak is a steak and it costs roughly the same everywhere. But if you sell it as 

Grill Masters Sweet & Smoky BBQ Angus Beef

You can add a beautifully designed label, market it in ads, and all the stuff you add it (salt water, coloring, additives) to increase the weight, so you can charge much more

Selling ultra processed food is a much better business to be in than selling unprocessed food (boring and no profit margin)

Thank capitalism for this!

An example is a type of meat my parents used to eat in the Netherlands, it was unprocessed then, and is now sold as ultra processed full of preservatives, emulsifiers, coloring and additives, and my parents have no idea because it looks roughly the same. It makes them sick though

Also yogurt, I grew up and it was just you know, yogurt, fermented milk, classified as NOVA 1 unprocessed. But modern yogurt isn't that anymore. A premium brand I used to buy called OIKOS by Danone, used to have 2 ingredients: milk and fermentation bacteria. Now it's some milk, a bit of cream, a lot of milk powder (with dubious origins) and fermentation bacteria to save money but the price went up! And that's the plain one. The flavored yogurts are full of artificial sweeteners, emulsifiers, additives etc.

So you can't really trust your eyes anymore to judge if food is clean or not, because most of it has been turned into processed or ultra processed to save money and/or market to you to sell for a higher price

When in doubt, try the NOVA scale

People asked if this meal is nutritionally complete, how on earth can you get all the nutrients you need from just this meal?

Well yes you can if you add some more things:
- Skyr (protein, calcium, B12, probiotics) with cinnamon, squeezed lemon juice and strawberries (vitamin C + fiber + polyphenols)
- Brussels sprouts (vitamin C + fiber + beneficial sulfur)
- Sunlight (go walk or sit outside for vitamin D ~15-30 min in late afternoon at low UV index)

The rest is already there:
- Steak (protein for muscle repair + strength, iron, zinc, B12, CoQ10, 
- 20g/day of 92% dark chocolate (flavanols, antioxidants, minerals, healthy fats)
- Black coffee (caffeine, antioxidants, lowers risk of cancer)
- 2 bananas (pottasium, natural carbs, fiber, B6)

Only thing missing here would be omega-3 from fish or eggs!
